problems.form_value: CON gpt_con vs CON low_con and CON gpt_con vs CON high_con, both coded ai_vs_active and with_ai, as randomized estimates. The form's what_was_assigned says the seed-set step is not stated as random, and its measure_detail leaves open which ideas were rated, but the coded values stay.
problems.source_says: Two checks fail. (a) The seed set is the between-participant factor, and the document never says it was assigned at random: Figure 1 says 'assigned between participants', and Section 4.3 calls the sub-arms 'unevenly assigned'. (b) As reported, the contrast rates seed content by its source. Section 4.1 compares 'GPT-4 ideas' with 'the uncreative human set' and 'the highly creative human set'. Section 3.4 compares crowd originality 'on the curated non-interactive sets' with the two researchers' curation ratings (r = .54), which reads most directly as crowd ratings of the seed ideas themselves. On that reading the conditions differ only in whose ideas get rated (GPT-4's or humans'), which is an AI-versus-human comparison (question none). On either reading the contrast is not a randomized test of AI assistance.
problems.quote: In the non-interactive condition, GPT-4 ideas were rated more original than the uncreative human set but less than the highly creative human set.
problems.locator: p. 4, Section 4.1; p. 3, Section 3.2 (Non-interactive baselines); p. 4, Section 3.4 (Rating protocol); p. 3, Figure 1 ('CON seed sets · assigned between participants'); p. 6, Section 4.3

problems.form_value: ai_vs_active: CON gpt_con (seen in the first session) vs CON high_con (seen in the first session), as a randomized estimate
problems.source_says: The contrast compares people by the seed set they read in a first CON session. The only randomized factor is the session order, which decides who had CON first. Which seed set a person read was 'assigned between participants', and the document never says this step was random. The authors call the sub-arms unevenly assigned and the finding exploratory. Without a statement of random allocation, the contrast does not support a randomized code.
problems.quote: Because CON sub-arms were unevenly assigned, we report this as an exploratory but directionally consistent finding that we are currently replicating in a larger sample.
problems.locator: p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 3, Figure 1 (subtitle and seed-set row, 'assigned between participants')

problems.source_says: One of the three seed sets pooled into CON is '16 GPT-4-only ideas' 'generated by the GPT-4 backend', and Figure 1 prints n = 21 for each set. So about one-third of CON sessions supplied AI-generated material. The form spec's other_aid covers web search, human-written examples, and human partners, which fits only the two human sets. The arm description discloses the mix and the schema has no mixed value, but the coded value does not hold for the whole arm. As a result, the GPT vs CON contrast (S1-O2) compares a GPT-4 partner with a control in which some people read GPT-4 ideas.
problems.quote: In the CON condition, participants were shown one of three pre-rated sets of 16 ideas: highly creative human ideas, uncreative human ideas, or GPT-4-only ideas.
problems.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2 (Non-interactive baselines); p. 3, Figure 1 (gpt_con box, n = 21); form-spec.md, field note on arms[].ai

problems.source_says: The codebook defines open_chat as free use of a chatbot. The document describes a constrained partner: server-enforced strict turn-taking, a prompt that limits each reply to one idea in one sentence, and a filter that rejects replies overlapping more than 50 percent with any earlier message. The participant and the model trade ideas under a 4-minute limit. The model works as a constrained ideation partner, not as a general chatbot the participant can use freely. The form's own note calls open_chat only 'the closest role code'. The code 'other', with this description, fits the codebook better. This does not affect criterion 1.
problems.quote: The AI’s prompt added behavioral guardrails identified in piloting to neutralize model-side asymmetries (verbosity, meta-commentary): one idea per turn, omit boilerplate preambles, single-sentence responses.
problems.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1 (AI configuration); creativity-codebook.md, Section 6 (AI role)

confirmed.statement: (a) The text states random order in its own words: 'Each participant completed three co-creation sessions within-subject in randomized order: human–human (HUM), human–GPT-4 (GPT), and non-interactive (CON for “constant”).' The form's assignment quote is verbatim, and randomized = yes is right for the session order.

(a, e) Figure 1 says the same three times. The subtitle reads 'Every participant runs the session loop three times — once per partner condition — in randomized order.' The loop panel reads 'Repeats × 3 — once per partner, order randomized'. The printed caption reads 'Each participant (N = 62) runs three randomized 4-minute co-creation sessions'. The form's quote of the subtitle is verbatim.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Figure 1 (image text, read from the embedded 1794 x 1345 image); Figure 1 caption, pp. 3-4

confirmed.statement: (e) The design is within-person, so a randomized order is what criterion 1 asks for. Figure 1 reads 'Within-subjects · every participant gets all three' and '62 participants × 3 sessions'. Unit within_person_order and structure mixed are right, because the CON seed set varied between participants ('Between-subjects · 1 of 3 sets'). Arm n_randomized = 62 for GPT, HUM, and CON (pooled) follows. Figure 3 prints subject-level n of CON 32 and 30, GPT 32 and 29, and HUM 32 and 30, as the arm descriptions say.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Figure 1; p. 6, Figure 3 (image text, read from the embedded 1317 x 888 image)

confirmed.statement: (b) What the GPT condition assigns is a live GPT-4 partner for the participant's own ideation. Two players 'generate uses for a target object together in a shared chat interface under a fixed time limit and matched instructions', and after each chat 'participants curated the “best” creative uses inspired by the chat in a separate survey tab'. GPT and HUM differ in the partner during the participant's own work, not only in whose output gets rated.

(b) Caveat for the outcome lens, no change in this lens. The rated pool is '1,928 ideas', '62 participants × 3 sessions', 'generated in chat + curated' (Figure 1 data-flow row), and Section 1.1 gives '1,928 ideas from 62 participants with 6× redundant originality ratings'. The document does not say whether GPT-4's own chat turns are in the GPT arm's rated pool (form open question 1). The embedded Figure 1 image also holds a second caption that the printed page covers ('The 1,928 ideas are rated 6× each by 225 Prolific workers'). It is not part of the visible document.
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Section 1.1; p. 3, Figure 1 data-flow row; embedded Figure 1 image, bottom strip, covered on the printed page

confirmed.statement: (c) The tool is a large language model: 'The GPT partner used gpt-4 via OpenAI’s chat-completions API with temperature = 0.7, max_tokens = 3000, and server-enforced strict turn-taking.' Participants are 'explicitly informed of partner identity (human or AI)'. ai_tool.name_model and the GPT arm's generative_ai code are right.

(d) The HUM comparison arm matches the form. Figure 1 describes HUM as 'Human × Human', 'live partner', 'two people in shared chat', and the text says 'Human–human interactions use the same interface with naturally occurring turn-taking'. The form spec puts human partners under other_aid, and codebook Section 5 lists 'a human partner' under ai_vs_active, so GPT vs HUM = ai_vs_active (S1-O1) is right.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Figure 1 (HUM box); p. 2, Section 3.1; form-spec.md, field note on arms[].ai; creativity-codebook.md, Section 5

confirmed.statement: The rest of what_was_assigned matches the text. Target objects: 'book, fork, tin can; counterbalanced' (Figure 1: 'counterbalanced ×3'). Solo AUT: half of the participants did it before the sessions and 'the other half completed it after', with no allocation method stated. Seed sets: 'assigned between participants', never called random, and 'unevenly assigned'. In the full text, 'random' appears only for the session order, for the design of Maier et al., for random forests, and for random effects.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2; p. 3, Figure 1; p. 6, Section 4.3; full text, pp. 1-8

confirmed.statement: The seed-set arms match Figure 1: gpt_con '16 GPT-4-only ideas' (generative_ai), and high_con '16 highly creative human ideas' and low_con '16 uncreative human ideas', both 'drawn from Stevenson et al. 2022' (other_aid), each with printed n = 21. Their n_randomized = null is right: no count at assignment is given, and 3 x 21 = 63 does not match N = 62.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Figure 1 seed-set row; p. 4, Figure 1 text alternative ('~21 participants each')

confirmed.statement: preregistered = not_stated is right. The document mentions no preregistration. The conclusion calls the platform a 'pre-registerable testbed', and the confirmatory outsourcing test is 'currently in progress'.

Caveat, no code change. The document does not describe how the order was randomized. On the platform, 'Environment variables control LLM backend, prompts, condition assignment, task items, chat length, and response wait times', and a HUM session needs two participants in HUM at the same time. So the unit of order randomization (person, pair, or lab session) is not stated. The form's open questions already raise the dyad issue.

summary: The core coding holds: the document says each of 62 students did a GPT-4-partner session, a human-partner session, and a non-interactive session 'in randomized order' (p. 3, Section 3.2; Figure 1), so GPT vs HUM is a randomized within-person comparison of an LLM partner with a human partner, and criterion 1 stands. The coding is still refuted on details: S1-O3 and S1-O4 carry randomized codes for seed-set contrasts that the paper never calls random ('unevenly assigned', p. 6), S1-O3 as reported rates GPT-4 seed ideas against human seed ideas, the pooled CON arm is coded other_aid although about one-third of it read GPT-4 ideas, and open_chat overstates a strictly turn-taking, one-idea-per-turn partner.
